overview: The Samnites were Oscan-speaking communities of central and southern Italy, including Samnium. Their history includes fortified settlements, skilled builders and long struggles with Rome. The map’s approximate 500 to 323 BCE coverage is only part of that story; several objects below come from later Samnite communities.

periods.title: The map’s early window
periods.summary: This imported outline approximates part of ancient Samnium. It does not establish the borders of one permanently united kingdom, and its endpoint does not mark the disappearance of Samnite people.

periods.title: Later communities and Roman expansion
periods.summary: Later houses, sanctuaries and inscriptions reveal continued Samnite life through changing relations with Rome. The temple-theatre at Pietrabbondante belongs to this later history, beyond the map’s displayed interval.

sections.title: A home with colour, food and work

items.text: At Monte Vairano, stone walls enclosed a hilltop settlement with gates and homes. Beside the southern gate, archaeologists excavated a house with red plaster above a black base and a floor made from lime and crushed terracotta. Ancient interiors could be colourful even when their ruins look grey.

Coins beneath that house’s floor date the floor to between 214 and 150 BCE. This is later than the map’s Samnite window. A coin lost or buried during building can help date a room, rather like finding a dated newspaper under an old floorboard.

The house contained cups, plates, cooking pans, lamps and loom weights. A storage vessel still held farro, a kind of wheat, and legumes. These finds bring cooking, storing food and making cloth into the same household story, although they cannot identify every person who performed those jobs.

Excavators also found a deep circular cistern at the settlement, with walls made using broken roof tiles. Water storage was a practical engineering concern. This evidence does not tell us that each home had a private bathroom or a flush toilet; a cistern alone cannot answer the toilet question.

sections.title: What can bones tell us about dinner?

items.text: Researchers studied carbon and nitrogen in human remains from Opi Val Fondillo, a community of the sixth and fifth centuries BCE. Their results suggest a diet largely based on land-grown foods, with relatively limited animal protein for many sampled people. These are long-term dietary clues, not a recovered weekly menu.

Some people had different nitrogen results, including differences between male and female samples. The researchers discuss food access alongside health and physiological explanations. It would be too confident to turn those measurements into a rule that every Samnite family always served identical portions, or always favoured one person at dinner.

sections.title: Public life with unusually good seats

items.text: Pietrabbondante was a major sanctuary of the Pentri Samnites. Its temple-theatre complex, built around the late second and early first centuries BCE, served religious and political purposes. Public worship, meetings and decisions about a community’s affairs could happen in connected spaces. This impressive later complex postdates the imported map window.

The theatre preserves stone seats with shaped backs and armrests carved as winged lions’ paws. Someone thought seriously about sitting comfortably, even without cushions surviving to prove it. A nearby public residence accommodated important priests and magistrates visiting for religious and political gatherings.

sections.title: Written language: a signature made with a shoe

items.text: A roof tile from Pietrabbondante, dated around 100 BCE, carries four shoeprints and two short messages, one in Oscan and one in Latin. Linguist Katherine McDonald interprets them as the work of two enslaved women, or possibly freedwomen, who handled wet clay tiles. The writing preserves a tiny moment in working life.

A short Oscan sample is “segnatted. plavtad”, meaning “signed with a footprint”. This is a Roman-letter transliteration of an inscription originally written in the Central Oscan alphabet. Forget a fancy signature: this worker left a shoeprint. The tile is later than the map’s displayed Samnite period.

The paired inscriptions show that these particular workers could write sentences. They do not tell us how they learned, whether they attended a school, or how common literacy was among other women. McDonald also notes uncertainty about whether Detfri, one word in the inscription, is a personal name or a designation.

Oscan was a language, not just one alphabet. Writers used different alphabets derived from Etruscan, Greek or Latin traditions in different regions and periods. Surviving texts appear on pottery, stone and metal, including dedications and legal or religious documents. A language could travel between materials as well as scripts.

sections.title: Rome won wars, but people kept living

items.text: In 290 BCE, after further Roman campaigns, the remaining Samnite opponents sought peace. A recent study describes their likely subordination within Rome’s alliance system, while stressing gaps in the ancient accounts. Losing military independence did not prevent later generations from building the houses and sanctuary described here.

Samnites later participated in the Social War against Rome, which began in 91 BCE. Roman citizenship expanded during the conflict, although some Samnite and Lucanian resistance continued. Political rights and alliances changed through a violent process; there was no single day on which an entire people simply vanished.

ending.text: Roman expansion gradually changed Samnite political independence, alliances and citizenship. Peace in 290 BCE was followed by further conflicts, including the Social War centuries later. The map stops at 323 BCE because of its imported coverage, not because Samnite communities ended in that year.
